messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 69
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Agricultural Worker
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 67

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly, Public Transport: Bus riding, Certain Conversation Topics: Certain conversation topics
  Maladaptive Strategies: Substance Use: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs, Worst Case Rehearsal: mentally rehearse worst case scenarios to feel prepared, Avoid People: avoid other people
  Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Martha is a sixty-nine-year-old agricultural worker who has been married for over forty years. She came to therapy reluctantly, at the urging of her daughter, after her PCL-5 score of 67 indicated severe posttraumatic symptoms. For decades, Martha had managed to keep the assault locked away, but in the past year, it had begun leaking through the cracks of her carefully constructed life.

The assault happened when Martha was twenty-two, working the early shift at a produce packing plant. She had stayed late to clean a conveyor belt, and a supervisor she had trusted cornered her in the back storage room. She still remembered the smell of diesel and rotting onions, the feel of concrete against her cheek, the way his belt buckle pressed into her lower back. She told no one. She went home, showered, and went to work the next day. She had come to believe, in the years that followed, that she should have been able to stop it—that she should have seen it coming, should have fought harder, should have been a different kind of woman. That belief had calcified into something harder: she could not rely on herself. If she could not protect herself from a man she knew, in a building she worked in every day, then she could not trust her own judgment about anything.

The memory did not stay buried. It came to her suddenly, without warning, usually when she was least prepared—while washing dishes, or in the middle of the night, or, most troublingly, on the bus. Public transport had become a nightmare. Every time a man sat too close, every time the bus lurched and someone’s arm brushed against hers, the memory surged back with full sensory force. She had stopped riding the bus unless absolutely necessary. Her husband drove her to the fields now, but that meant she had to coordinate her shifts around his schedule, and sometimes she was late. Her supervisor had noticed. Martha had started making excuses.

Certain conversation topics could trigger her as well. When other women in the packing shed talked about their husbands, or when someone mentioned a late shift, or when a male coworker made a joke she could not quite hear, Martha’s stomach would drop. She had learned to keep her head down, to move away, to pretend she had not heard. She had become an expert at disappearing in plain sight. But the cost was loneliness. She felt, with a certainty that had only grown stronger over the decades, that she was permanently an outsider now—set apart from other people by something they could not see and she could not explain. She was certain that if anyone knew what had happened, they would see her differently, so she kept everyone at a distance.

To manage the constant dread, Martha had developed habits that made sense to her but had slowly shrunk her world. She checked behind her constantly—when walking to the car, when entering a room, when standing at the sink. She only felt safe in a very limited number of places: her own kitchen, the back corner of the packing shed where she had a clear view of the door, her daughter’s living room if her son-in-law was not home. Anywhere else, she was on high alert, scanning for exits, for faces, for anything that felt wrong. She drank most evenings—just enough wine to take the edge off, she told herself—and she had begun rehearsing worst-case scenarios in her head before any outing, running through what she would do if a man approached, if the bus broke down, if someone cornered her again. It was exhausting, but it felt like the only way to stay safe.

What finally brought Martha to therapy was not the fear itself, but the isolation. Her husband had grown frustrated with her refusals to attend family gatherings, her daughter had cried on the phone, and Martha had realized she could not remember the last time she had felt truly at ease in another person’s company. She was afraid of what therapy might uncover—afraid that talking about it would make the memories worse, afraid that she would be judged, afraid that she was too old to change. But she was also, beneath the fear, hoping for something she could barely name: a way to feel less alone in her own life.
